---
title: "A typical session"
description: "The order an agent works in, from opening a project through placing, changing and checking clips to saving and exporting."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

An agent works in Frame Job the way you do: bring the media in, place it, change it, look at the result, then save and export. What's different is that it can't see the window, so it reads the project for the ids it needs and renders a frame to check each step.

<AtAGlance
  tools={['new_project', 'open_project', 'get_project', 'import_media', 'add_clip', 'render_frame', 'save_project', 'export', 'export_status']}
/>

## Work through a session

<Steps>

1. **Open.** Call `open_project` with a path, or `new_project` for a blank 1920 × 1080, 30 fps project with one track. See [Tools: projects and history](/mcp/tools-projects/).

2. **Read.** Call `get_project`. It answers the canvas, the playhead and every id. Every other tool names things by those ids.

3. **Import.** Call `import_media` with the file's path. It answers the new `media` id and what the file holds: its kind, duration, size, frame rate, and whether it has video, sound or transparency. The file is in the project now, but not on the timeline.

4. **Place.** Call `add_clip` with `track`, `media` and `at`. The answer lists the new clip's id under `new_clips`.

5. **Change.** Use the edit tools. Each call is one undo step. See [All tools](/mcp/tools/).

6. **Check.** Call `render_frame` at the moment that matters, and look at the picture. Do this before and after an edit.

7. **Save.** Call `save_project`, with a `path` the first time. It answers once the package is really on disk.

8. **Export.** Call `export` with a `preset` and a `path`. It answers at once with an `export_id`. Then call `export_status` until `status` is `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`.

</Steps>

Steps 5 and 6 are the loop. An edit that comes back `ok` says the project changed, and only a frame says it looks right. If it doesn't, `undo` takes the last step back.

## See one from start to finish

Here's a short session, each call with its arguments. Times are in ticks, 600,000 to the second, so `1200000` is 2 s.

```json
new_project   { "path": "~/Movies/Talk.framejob" }
get_project   { }
import_media  { "path": "~/Movies/talk.mov" }
add_clip      { "track": 1, "media": 2, "at": 0 }
split         { "clips": [3], "at": 1200000 }
render_frame  { "t": 1200000, "max_width": 960 }
save_project  { }
export        { "preset": "h264", "path": "~/Movies/Talk.mp4" }
export_status { "export_id": 1 }
```

`media` and `clips` here stand for the ids the earlier answers gave. Read them from each answer rather than guessing, because ids come from one number series that clips, tracks, markers and media all share. See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).

`save_project` needs no `path` here because `new_project` was given one. A project made without one stays an untitled draft until the first `save_project` that names a path.

## Follow the export

`export` puts the job on the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) and returns. It doesn't wait for the file.

`export_status` never waits either, so pause between calls. While the job runs, its answer has `progress`, from 0 to 1. When `status` is `done`, the answer says what the file holds, including its size in `bytes`, its settings and its loudness. `failed` and `cancelled` come with a `reason`.

To stop a job, call `cancel_export`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

## Good to know

- Tools act on the frontmost project. With more than one open, pass `project`, the path `get_project` reports. See [How tool calls behave](/mcp/tool-calls/).
- A call that can't do what it's asked comes back with the reason, and the project stays as it was. See [What a call answers](/mcp/what-a-call-answers/).
- `render_frame` and `export` differ inside a [nest](/mcp/nests/). With a nest open, `render_frame` draws the nest, but `export` still writes the whole timeline.
- `export` replaces a file already at the path, and adds the container's extension when the path has none.
- `unsaved_changes` in `get_project` says whether there's anything still to save.

## Related

- [Read the project: get_project](/mcp/get-project/)
- [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/)
- [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/)
- [Patches](/mcp/patches/)

5. **Change.** Use the edit tools. Each call is one undo step. See [All tools](/mcp/tools/).

6. **Check.** Call `render_frame` at the moment that matters, and look at the picture. Do this before and after an edit.

7. **Save.** Call `save_project`, with a `path` the first time. It answers once the package is really on disk.

8. **Export.** Call `export` with a `preset` and a `path`. It answers at once with an `export_id`. Then call `export_status` until `status` is `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`.

</Steps>

Steps 5 and 6 are the loop. An edit that comes back `ok` says the project changed, and only a frame says it looks right. If it doesn't, `undo` takes the last step back.

## See one from start to finish

Here's a short session, each call with its arguments. Times are in ticks, 600,000 to the second, so `1200000` is 2 s.

```json
new_project   { "path": "~/Movies/Talk.framejob" }
get_project   { }
import_media  { "path": "~/Movies/talk.mov" }
add_clip      { "track": 1, "media": 2, "at": 0 }
split         { "clips": [3], "at": 1200000 }
render_frame  { "t": 1200000, "max_width": 960 }
save_project  { }
export        { "preset": "h264", "path": "~/Movies/Talk.mp4" }
export_status { "export_id": 1 }
```

`media` and `clips` here stand for the ids the earlier answers gave. Read them from each answer rather than guessing, because ids come from one number series that clips, tracks, markers and media all share. See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).

`save_project` needs no `path` here because `new_project` was given one. A project made without one stays an untitled draft until the first `save_project` that names a path.

## Follow the export

`export` puts the job on the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) and returns. It doesn't wait for the file.

`export_status` never waits either, so pause between calls. While the job runs, its answer has `progress`, from 0 to 1. When `status` is `done`, the answer says what the file holds, including its size in `bytes`, its settings and its loudness. `failed` and `cancelled` come with a `reason`.

To stop a job, call `cancel_export`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

## Good to know

- Tools act on the frontmost project. With more than one open, pass `project`, the path `get_project` reports. See [How tool calls behave](/mcp/tool-calls/).
- A call that can't do what it's asked comes back with the reason, and the project stays as it was. See [What a call answers](/mcp/what-a-call-answers/).
- `render_frame` and `export` differ inside a [nest](/mcp/nests/). With a nest open, `render_frame` draws the nest, but `export` still writes the whole timeline.
- `export` replaces a file already at the path, and adds the container's extension when the path has none.
- `unsaved_changes` in `get_project` says whether there's anything still to save.

## Related

- [Read the project: get_project](/mcp/get-project/)
- [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/)
- [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/)
- [Patches](/mcp/patches/)

---
title: "Read the project: get_project"
description: "What get_project answers: the project's contents and ids, the playhead and selection, its graphics, a file's Camera Log, and the report while a nest is open."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`get_project` answers the whole project as JSON, the same document every edit changes. Read it first, because every other tool names things by the ids it reports.

<AtAGlance tools="get_project" />

## Read the project

The only argument is `project`, the path of the open project to read. Leave it out for the frontmost one. The call changes nothing.

Three things hold for everything it answers:

- Times are ticks, 600,000 to the second.
- Clip, track, marker and media ids share one number series, so an id means one thing on its own.
- `tracks[0]` is the back of the layer stack, the bottom lane of the timeline.

See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).

## What it answers

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `project` | The project itself. See [below](#what-project-holds). |
| `path` | Where the project is saved, or `null` if it never has been. |
| `name` | The project's name, or `Untitled`. |
| `unsaved_changes` | `true` when there's something to save. |
| `duration` | The timeline's length in ticks. |
| `playhead` | The playhead, in ticks. |
| `selection` | The ids of the selected clips, in order. |
| `in_out_range` | `start` and `end` in ticks. Only there when a range is set. |
| `scope` | The id of the [open nest](#the-report-while-a-nest-is-open), or `null` at the timeline. |
| `missing_media` | The ids of media whose file has moved. Only there when one has. `relink_media` points one at its new place. |
| `graphics` | The project's [graphic modules](#the-graphics-summary). |
| `note` | A reminder of the rules above, in a sentence or two. |

`playhead`, `selection` and `in_out_range` are the app's own state. They aren't saved with the project, and setting them isn't an undo step.

## What `project` holds

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `canvas` | The picture's settings. See the next table. |
| `media` | Every file in the project, whether or not a clip uses it. |
| `tracks` | The timeline's tracks, back to front. |
| `clips` | The timeline's clips. |
| `markers` | The timeline's markers. |
| `nests` | Every nest, each with its own `id`, `name`, `width`, `height`, `tracks` and `clips`. |
| `next_id` | The id the next new thing will take. |
| `version` | The project file's version. |

| `canvas` key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The canvas size in pixels. |
| `fps` | The frame rate as `[num, den]`, so 29.97 fps is `[30000, 1001]`. |
| `background` | The canvas background. |
| `fit_new_clips` | Whether a new clip is scaled to fit when its source is bigger than the canvas. |
| `timecode_frames` | Whether timecode reads `HH:MM:SS:FF` rather than `HH:MM:SS.mmm`. |
| `output` | `hlg` in an [HDR project](/hdr/hdr-projects/). Left out in an SDR project. |
| `blending` | `linear` with [linear-light blending](/hdr/linear-light/) on. Left out otherwise. |

A media entry has `id`, `path`, `kind`, `duration`, `width`, `height`, `fps`, `has_video`, `has_audio` and `has_alpha`, and sometimes more: `original` for a copy, `color` for [its colour setting](#camera-log-readback), `speech` for saved speech spans and `cursor` for a recording's cursor file.

A clip has `id`, `track`, `start`, `duration`, `source`, `enabled`, `speed` and `actions`. What it shows sits in `video`, `audio`, `text`, `shape` or `graphic`. `source.kind` says what kind of clip it is, and a nest clip's `source.project` is the id of the nest it shows.

## The graphics summary

`graphics` is a list with one entry for each module in the project's graphics folder, in name order:

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The module's name. |
| `revision` | The module's revision. It changes when the text does. |
| `ok` | `true` when the module compiles. |
| `clips` | The ids of the clips drawn by it, on the timeline and in every nest. |

`ok: false` is the first sign that a graphic clip will draw its error card. See [Graphics with an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/).

The list is empty in a project with no modules, and in a project that has no window.

## Camera Log readback

A file's colour setting is in `color` on its media entry. A file with no setting has no `color`, and each key below appears only when it's set.

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `log` | The curve: `apple_log`, `apple_log2`, `slog3`, `vlog`, `canon_log2` or `canon_log3`. |
| `gamut` | The gamut: `bt2020`, `apple_wide_gamut`, `s_gamut3_cine`, `s_gamut3`, `v_gamut` or `cinema_gamut`. |
| `lut` | The media id of a [LUT](/hdr/log-luts/) used as the conversion, in place of `log`. |
| `detected` | `true` when Frame Job read the setting from the file at import. |
| `pq` | An HDR10 file's peak: `file` is what import read, in cd/m², `from` is where it read it (`max_cll` or `mastering_display`), and `peak` is an override. An empty `pq` still marks the file as HDR10. |

`detected: true` is how to tell a setting the file declared from one a person or an agent chose. Setting the Camera Log with `set_media_color` replaces it and drops `detected`. See [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/).

## The report while a nest is open

While `set_scope` has a nest open, `get_project` reports the nest as if it were the project, so the ids you read are the ones the next edit can name.

- `project.tracks` and `project.clips` are the nest's own.
- `project.canvas` has the nest's fixed size. Its other settings are the project's.
- `project.markers` is empty, because a nest has no markers.
- `project.media` and `project.nests` are still the whole project's, but the open nest's own row under `nests` has no tracks or clips, because they're at the top level here.
- `duration`, `playhead`, `selection` and `in_out_range` are the nest's, measured from its own zero.

Two more keys say where you are:

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `scope_clip` | The nest clip it was entered through. |
| `scope_path` | The trail of nests from the timeline, one `{nest, clip, name}` for each level. |

`scope` is the nest's id, the same number an edit's `scope` argument takes. At the timeline `scope` is `null`, and the two keys above aren't there.

`render_frame` follows the same view and draws the nest at its own size. Opening a nest is a change of view, not an undo step. See [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/).

## Related

- [Tools: projects and history](/mcp/tools-projects/)
- [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/)
- [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/)
- [A typical session](/mcp/typical-session/)

---
title: "Check the picture: render_frame"
description: "Render one frame of the finished timeline so an agent can see its work, choose the file it writes, draw grade and HDR variants, and measure the scopes."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`render_frame` draws one frame of the finished timeline, so an agent can see what it has done. It goes through the same composition and compositor an export uses, so the picture is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Save Frame…"
  keys="⌥⌘E"
  tools="render_frame"
/>

## Render a frame

With no arguments it draws the frame under the playhead at the canvas's size and writes a PNG to a temporary file.

```json
{ "t": 1200000, "path": "~/Desktop/shot.png", "max_width": 960 }
```

The picture comes back two ways: as an image the model can see, and as a file on disk. The text beside it says what was drawn and ends by naming the file:

```
Frame at 1200000 ticks of a 1920×1080 px canvas, rendered at 960×540 px. Written to /Users/you/Desktop/shot.png.
```

It uses the same writer as [**File ▸ Save Frame…**](/export/save-frame/), so a PNG from either one is identical, byte for byte.

With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open, it draws that nest at its own size, from its own zero, without the nest clip's position, scale or opacity. It takes no `scope`, so open the nest with `set_scope` to look inside.

| Argument | Type | Required | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`t`](#t) | integer | No | The moment to render, in ticks. | The playhead |
| [`path`](#path) | string | No | Where to write the file. | A temporary file |
| [`format`](#format) | string | No | `png`, `jpeg` or `heic`. | From the path, else `png` |
| [`max_width`](#max_width) | integer | No | Caps the width in pixels, 16 to 8192. | The canvas's width |
| [`burn_in_timecode`](#burn_in_timecode) | boolean | No | Draws the project timecode over the picture. | `false` |
| [`ungraded`](#ungraded) | boolean | No | Draws every clip as if it weren't graded. | `false` |
| [`selection`](#selection) | integer | No | Draws what an adjustment clip's qualifier selects. | None |
| [`sdr_version`](#sdr_version) | boolean | No | Draws an HDR project's SDR version. | `false` |
| [`waveform`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the waveform. | `false` |
| [`parade`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the RGB parade. | `false` |
| [`histogram`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the histogram. | `false` |
| [`vectorscope`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | boolean | No | Also measures the vectorscope. | `false` |
| [`vectorscope_zoom`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | integer | No | 1, 2 or 4. Needs `vectorscope`. | 1 |
| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to act on. | The frontmost project |

## Choose the moment and the file

### `t`

The moment to render, in ticks, 600,000 to the second. It's rounded to the project's frame grid. Leave it out for the playhead. A time before zero draws the first frame, and a time past the end is refused.

With a nest open, `t` and the playhead are the nest's own time.

### `path`

Where to write the file, for example `~/Desktop/shot.png`. The folder must already exist, because Frame Job won't create one. An empty `path` is refused.

Leave it out for a temporary file. Either way, the last sentence of the text names the file written.

### `format`

The kind of file to write.

| `format` | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| `png` | Lossless, keeping the canvas's transparency. |
| `jpeg` | Quality 0.9. JPEG has no transparency, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black, and the text always says so. |
| `heic` | Quality 0.9, keeping the canvas's transparency. |

With no `format`, the path's extension decides, and `.jpg` and `.jpeg` both mean JPEG. Any other path writes a PNG.

An explicit `format` wins, and the path's extension is replaced rather than added to, so `{"path": "shot.jpg", "format": "png"}` writes `shot.png`. Only an extension Frame Job knows is replaced: `Talk v1.2` becomes `Talk v1.2.png`, not `Talk v1.png`. A JPEG always ends `.jpg`, so `shot.jpeg` is written as `shot.jpg`.

`jpg` also works as a `format`, and capitals don't matter.

### `max_width`

Caps the image's width in pixels, from 16 to 8192. The picture keeps its shape and is never made larger than the canvas. Leave it out for the canvas's own size.

A smaller frame is quicker to send and to look at. The [scopes](#measure-the-frame) measure the frame as written, so their counts cover fewer pixels too.

## Change what's drawn

These four draw something other than the plain picture. The view switches in the window never reach this tool or an export, so an agent asks here.

### `burn_in_timecode`

Draws the project timecode over the picture, on top of everything, as the export sheet's **Burn in timecode** does. It's the project's own timecode, in the toolbar's spelling. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/).

### `ungraded`

Draws every clip as if it weren't graded: Light, Color, wheels and curves neutral, and no look. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Ungraded** gives. See [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/).

### `selection`

Takes an adjustment clip's id and draws what its qualifier selects, in place of grading. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Selection** gives.

- White is fully graded, and black is untouched.
- It's the blurred selection when the qualifier has a blur, and it's multiplied by any matte cutting the clip.
- The clip's strength isn't applied.
- Every layer in front of the clip is left out.
- Where the clip isn't on the frame, the picture is black.

Frame Job won't do this for any other kind of clip. See [Qualifiers](/color/qualifiers/).

### `sdr_version`

Draws an [HDR project's](/hdr/hdr-projects/) SDR version, the picture **View ▸ Show SDR Version** gives. White titles come back near white, and highlights above reference white roll off. It's what the SDR exports and JPEG frames hold.

In an SDR project it changes nothing, and the frame comes out identical. See [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/).

## Measure the frame

Each scope argument measures the frame just rendered through the same analyser as the [**View ▸ Scopes**](/color/scopes/) panel, so the two can't count differently. The text gives the headline figures, and a JSON file beside the image holds the counts, named after it: `shot.png` gets `shot.png.waveform.json`.

The scopes read the frame as it was drawn, so `max_width`, `burn_in_timecode`, `ungraded` and `selection` all change what they count.

If the measurement can't run, the call comes back as an error, but the image is already written and the error names it: "Wrote … but its waveform could not be measured: the GPU pass did not run."

### `waveform`, `parade` and `histogram`

- **`waveform`** measures luma. The text gives the share of pixels clipping high and low.
- **`parade`** measures R′, G′ and B′ the way the waveform measures luma. The text gives the share clipping high and low for each channel.
- **`histogram`** counts R′, G′, B′ and Y′ at 256 levels. The text gives the share clipping high and low, read from Y′.

For example: "Waveform: highlights clipped in 0.4 % of pixels, shadows in 0.0 %; its 256 × 256 counts are in …". A pixel clips high at level 255 and low at level 0.

| JSON key | `waveform` | `parade` | `histogram` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The frame measured | The frame measured | The frame measured |
| `levels` | 256 | 256 | 256 |
| `columns` | 256 | 256 | |
| `counts` | 256 column bins, each 256 levels | The same, under `red`, `green` and `blue` | |
| `red`, `green`, `blue`, `luma` | | | 256 counts each |
| `clipped_high`, `clipped_low` | Pixels clipping | Pixels clipping, by channel | Pixels clipping, by Y′ |
| `marks_high`, `marks_low` | The column bins where at least 0.5 % of the column clips | The same, by channel | |
| `highlights`, `shadows` | Percentages | | Percentages |

### `vectorscope` and `vectorscope_zoom`

`vectorscope` measures Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral, bin 128. The text gives the share of pixels that are neutral.

`vectorscope_zoom` is 1, 2 or 4, like the 1×, 2× and 4× cells on a [vectorscope](/color/vectorscope/) slot, and it needs `vectorscope: true`. Zooming spreads a near-grey picture over more bins. At 2 and 4, a pixel off the plot isn't counted, and the text also gives the share that lie off it.

| JSON key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The frame measured. |

---
title: "Check the picture: render_frame"
description: "Render one frame of the finished timeline so an agent can see its work, choose the file it writes, draw grade and HDR variants, and measure the scopes."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`render_frame` draws one frame of the finished timeline, so an agent can see what it has done. It goes through the same composition and compositor an export uses, so the picture is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Save Frame…"
  keys="⌥⌘E"
  tools="render_frame"
/>

## Render a frame

With no arguments it draws the frame under the playhead at the canvas's size and writes a PNG to a temporary file.

```json
{ "t": 1200000, "path": "~/Desktop/shot.png", "max_width": 960 }
```

The picture comes back two ways: as an image the model can see, and as a file on disk. The text beside it says what was drawn and ends by naming the file:

```
Frame at 1200000 ticks of a 1920×1080 px canvas, rendered at 960×540 px. Written to /Users/you/Desktop/shot.png.
```

It uses the same writer as [**File ▸ Save Frame…**](/export/save-frame/), so a PNG from either one is identical, byte for byte.

With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open, it draws that nest at its own size, from its own zero, without the nest clip's position, scale or opacity. It takes no `scope`, so open the nest with `set_scope` to look inside.

| Argument | Type | Required | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`t`](#t) | integer | No | The moment to render, in ticks. | The playhead |
| [`path`](#path) | string | No | Where to write the file. | A temporary file |
| [`format`](#format) | string | No | `png`, `jpeg` or `heic`. | From the path, else `png` |
| [`max_width`](#max_width) | integer | No | Caps the width in pixels, 16 to 8192. | The canvas's width |
| [`burn_in_timecode`](#burn_in_timecode) | boolean | No | Draws the project timecode over the picture. | `false` |
| [`ungraded`](#ungraded) | boolean | No | Draws every clip as if it weren't graded. | `false` |
| [`selection`](#selection) | integer | No | Draws what an adjustment clip's qualifier selects. | None |
| [`sdr_version`](#sdr_version) | boolean | No | Draws an HDR project's SDR version. | `false` |
| [`waveform`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the waveform. | `false` |
| [`parade`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the RGB parade. | `false` |
| [`histogram`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the histogram. | `false` |
| [`vectorscope`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | boolean | No | Also measures the vectorscope. | `false` |
| [`vectorscope_zoom`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | integer | No | 1, 2 or 4. Needs `vectorscope`. | 1 |
| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to act on. | The frontmost project |

## Choose the moment and the file

### `t`

The moment to render, in ticks, 600,000 to the second. It's rounded to the project's frame grid. Leave it out for the playhead. A time before zero draws the first frame, and a time past the end is refused.

With a nest open, `t` and the playhead are the nest's own time.

### `path`

Where to write the file, for example `~/Desktop/shot.png`. The folder must already exist, because Frame Job won't create one. An empty `path` is refused.

Leave it out for a temporary file. Either way, the last sentence of the text names the file written.

### `format`

The kind of file to write.

| `format` | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| `png` | Lossless, keeping the canvas's transparency. |
| `jpeg` | Quality 0.9. JPEG has no transparency, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black, and the text always says so. |
| `heic` | Quality 0.9, keeping the canvas's transparency. |

With no `format`, the path's extension decides, and `.jpg` and `.jpeg` both mean JPEG. Any other path writes a PNG.

An explicit `format` wins, and the path's extension is replaced rather than added to, so `{"path": "shot.jpg", "format": "png"}` writes `shot.png`. Only an extension Frame Job knows is replaced: `Talk v1.2` becomes `Talk v1.2.png`, not `Talk v1.png`. A JPEG always ends `.jpg`, so `shot.jpeg` is written as `shot.jpg`.

`jpg` also works as a `format`, and capitals don't matter.

### `max_width`

Caps the image's width in pixels, from 16 to 8192. The picture keeps its shape and is never made larger than the canvas. Leave it out for the canvas's own size.

A smaller frame is quicker to send and to look at. The [scopes](#measure-the-frame) measure the frame as written, so their counts cover fewer pixels too.

## Change what's drawn

These four draw something other than the plain picture. The view switches in the window never reach this tool or an export, so an agent asks here.

### `burn_in_timecode`

Draws the project timecode over the picture, on top of everything, as the export sheet's **Burn in timecode** does. It's the project's own timecode, in the toolbar's spelling. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/).

### `ungraded`

Draws every clip as if it weren't graded: Light, Color, wheels and curves neutral, and no look. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Ungraded** gives. See [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/).

### `selection`

Takes an adjustment clip's id and draws what its qualifier selects, in place of grading. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Selection** gives.

- White is fully graded, and black is untouched.
- It's the blurred selection when the qualifier has a blur, and it's multiplied by any matte cutting the clip.
- The clip's strength isn't applied.
- Every layer in front of the clip is left out.
- Where the clip isn't on the frame, the picture is black.

Frame Job won't do this for any other kind of clip. See [Qualifiers](/color/qualifiers/).

### `sdr_version`

Draws an [HDR project's](/hdr/hdr-projects/) SDR version, the picture **View ▸ Show SDR Version** gives. White titles come back near white, and highlights above reference white roll off. It's what the SDR exports and JPEG frames hold.

In an SDR project it changes nothing, and the frame comes out identical. See [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/).

Each scope argument measures the frame just rendered through the same analyser as the [**View ▸ Scopes**](/color/scopes/) panel, so the two can't count differently. The text gives the headline figures, and a JSON file beside the image holds the counts, named after it: `shot.png` gets `shot.png.waveform.json`.

The scopes read the frame as it was drawn, so `max_width`, `burn_in_timecode`, `ungraded` and `selection` all change what they count.

If the measurement can't run, the call comes back as an error, but the image is already written and the error names it: "Wrote … but its waveform could not be measured: the GPU pass did not run."

### `waveform`, `parade` and `histogram`

- **`waveform`** measures luma. The text gives the share of pixels clipping high and low.
- **`parade`** measures R′, G′ and B′ the way the waveform measures luma. The text gives the share clipping high and low for each channel.
- **`histogram`** counts R′, G′, B′ and Y′ at 256 levels. The text gives the share clipping high and low, read from Y′.

For example: "Waveform: highlights clipped in 0.4 % of pixels, shadows in 0.0 %; its 256 × 256 counts are in …". A pixel clips high at level 255 and low at level 0.

| JSON key | `waveform` | `parade` | `histogram` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The frame measured | The frame measured | The frame measured |
| `levels` | 256 | 256 | 256 |
| `columns` | 256 | 256 | |
| `counts` | 256 column bins, each 256 levels | The same, under `red`, `green` and `blue` | |
| `red`, `green`, `blue`, `luma` | | | 256 counts each |
| `clipped_high`, `clipped_low` | Pixels clipping | Pixels clipping, by channel | Pixels clipping, by Y′ |
| `marks_high`, `marks_low` | The column bins where at least 0.5 % of the column clips | The same, by channel | |
| `highlights`, `shadows` | Percentages | | Percentages |

`vectorscope` measures Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral, bin 128. The text gives the share of pixels that are neutral.

`vectorscope_zoom` is 1, 2 or 4, like the 1×, 2× and 4× cells on a [vectorscope](/color/vectorscope/) slot, and it needs `vectorscope: true`. Zooming spreads a near-grey picture over more bins. At 2 and 4, a pixel off the plot isn't counted, and the text also gives the share that lie off it.

| JSON key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The frame measured. |
| `bins`, `centre` | 256 and 128. |
| `matrix`, `values` | `Rec. 709` and `encoded`. |
| `counts` | 256 arrays by Cr bin, each indexed by Cb bin. |
| `neutral` | Pixels in the neutral bin. |
| `zoom` | The zoom. |
| `off_plot` | Pixels left off the plot. Always 0 at 1. |
| `targets` | The six 75 % colour targets, `R`, `Mg`, `B`, `Cy`, `G` and `Yl`, each `[cb, cr]` in bins at this zoom, or `null` off the plot. |
| `skin_line_degrees` | The skin line's angle. |

---
title: "A typical session"
description: "The order an agent works in, from opening a project through placing, changing and checking clips to saving and exporting."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

An agent works in Frame Job the way you do: bring the media in, place it, change it, look at the result, then save and export. What's different is that it can't see the window, so it reads the project for the ids it needs and renders a frame to check each step.

<AtAGlance
  tools={['new_project', 'open_project', 'get_project', 'import_media', 'add_clip', 'render_frame', 'save_project', 'export', 'export_status']}
/>

## Work through a session

<Steps>

1. **Open.** Call `open_project` with a path, or `new_project` for a blank 1920 × 1080, 30 fps project with one track. See [Tools: projects and history](/mcp/tools-projects/).

2. **Read.** Call `get_project`. It answers the canvas, the playhead and every id. Every other tool names things by those ids.

3. **Import.** Call `import_media` with the file's path. It answers the new `media` id and what the file holds: its kind, duration, size, frame rate, and whether it has video, sound or transparency. The file is in the project now, but not on the timeline.

4. **Place.** Call `add_clip` with `track`, `media` and `at`. The answer lists the new clip's id under `new_clips`.

5. **Change.** Use the edit tools. Each call is one undo step. See [All tools](/mcp/tools/).

6. **Check.** Call `render_frame` at the moment that matters, and look at the picture. Do this before and after an edit.

7. **Save.** Call `save_project`, with a `path` the first time. It answers once the package is really on disk.

8. **Export.** Call `export` with a `preset` and a `path`. It answers at once with an `export_id`. Then call `export_status` until `status` is `done`, `failed` or `cancelled`.

</Steps>

Steps 5 and 6 are the loop. An edit that comes back `ok` says the project changed, and only a frame says it looks right. If it doesn't, `undo` takes the last step back.

## See one from start to finish

Here's a short session, each call with its arguments. Times are in ticks, 600,000 to the second, so `1200000` is 2 s.

```json
new_project   { "path": "~/Movies/Talk.framejob" }
get_project   { }
import_media  { "path": "~/Movies/talk.mov" }
add_clip      { "track": 1, "media": 2, "at": 0 }
split         { "clips": [3], "at": 1200000 }
render_frame  { "t": 1200000, "max_width": 960 }
save_project  { }
export        { "preset": "h264", "path": "~/Movies/Talk.mp4" }
export_status { "export_id": 1 }
```

`media` and `clips` here stand for the ids the earlier answers gave. Read them from each answer rather than guessing, because ids come from one number series that clips, tracks, markers and media all share. See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).

`save_project` needs no `path` here because `new_project` was given one. A project made without one stays an untitled draft until the first `save_project` that names a path.

## Follow the export

`export` puts the job on the [Export Queue](/export/export-queue/) and returns. It doesn't wait for the file.

`export_status` never waits either, so pause between calls. While the job runs, its answer has `progress`, from 0 to 1. When `status` is `done`, the answer says what the file holds, including its size in `bytes`, its settings and its loudness. `failed` and `cancelled` come with a `reason`.

To stop a job, call `cancel_export`. See [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/).

## Good to know

- Tools act on the frontmost project. With more than one open, pass `project`, the path `get_project` reports. See [How tool calls behave](/mcp/tool-calls/).
- A call that can't do what it's asked comes back with the reason, and the project stays as it was. See [What a call answers](/mcp/what-a-call-answers/).
- `render_frame` and `export` differ inside a [nest](/mcp/nests/). With a nest open, `render_frame` draws the nest, but `export` still writes the whole timeline.
- `export` replaces a file already at the path, and adds the container's extension when the path has none.
- `unsaved_changes` in `get_project` says whether there's anything still to save.

## Related

- [Read the project: get_project](/mcp/get-project/)
- [Check the picture: render_frame](/mcp/render-frame/)
- [Export: start, then poll](/mcp/export/)
- [Patches](/mcp/patches/)

---
title: "Read the project: get_project"
description: "What get_project answers: the project's contents and ids, the playhead and selection, its graphics, a file's Camera Log, and the report while a nest is open."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`get_project` answers the whole project as JSON, the same document every edit changes. Read it first, because every other tool names things by the ids it reports.

<AtAGlance tools="get_project" />

## Read the project

The only argument is `project`, the path of the open project to read. Leave it out for the frontmost one. The call changes nothing.

Three things hold for everything it answers:

- Times are ticks, 600,000 to the second.
- Clip, track, marker and media ids share one number series, so an id means one thing on its own.
- `tracks[0]` is the back of the layer stack, the bottom lane of the timeline.

See [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/).

## What it answers

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `project` | The project itself. See [below](#what-project-holds). |
| `path` | Where the project is saved, or `null` if it never has been. |
| `name` | The project's name, or `Untitled`. |
| `unsaved_changes` | `true` when there's something to save. |
| `duration` | The timeline's length in ticks. |
| `playhead` | The playhead, in ticks. |
| `selection` | The ids of the selected clips, in order. |
| `in_out_range` | `start` and `end` in ticks. Only there when a range is set. |
| `scope` | The id of the [open nest](#the-report-while-a-nest-is-open), or `null` at the timeline. |
| `missing_media` | The ids of media whose file has moved. Only there when one has. `relink_media` points one at its new place. |
| `graphics` | The project's [graphic modules](#the-graphics-summary). |
| `note` | A reminder of the rules above, in a sentence or two. |

`playhead`, `selection` and `in_out_range` are the app's own state. They aren't saved with the project, and setting them isn't an undo step.

## What `project` holds

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `canvas` | The picture's settings. See the next table. |
| `media` | Every file in the project, whether or not a clip uses it. |
| `tracks` | The timeline's tracks, back to front. |
| `clips` | The timeline's clips. |
| `markers` | The timeline's markers. |
| `nests` | Every nest, each with its own `id`, `name`, `width`, `height`, `tracks` and `clips`. |
| `next_id` | The id the next new thing will take. |
| `version` | The project file's version. |

| `canvas` key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The canvas size in pixels. |
| `fps` | The frame rate as `[num, den]`, so 29.97 fps is `[30000, 1001]`. |
| `background` | The canvas background. |
| `fit_new_clips` | Whether a new clip is scaled to fit when its source is bigger than the canvas. |
| `timecode_frames` | Whether timecode reads `HH:MM:SS:FF` rather than `HH:MM:SS.mmm`. |
| `output` | `hlg` in an [HDR project](/hdr/hdr-projects/). Left out in an SDR project. |
| `blending` | `linear` with [linear-light blending](/hdr/linear-light/) on. Left out otherwise. |

A media entry has `id`, `path`, `kind`, `duration`, `width`, `height`, `fps`, `has_video`, `has_audio` and `has_alpha`, and sometimes more: `original` for a copy, `color` for [its colour setting](#camera-log-readback), `speech` for saved speech spans and `cursor` for a recording's cursor file.

A clip has `id`, `track`, `start`, `duration`, `source`, `enabled`, `speed` and `actions`. What it shows sits in `video`, `audio`, `text`, `shape` or `graphic`. `source.kind` says what kind of clip it is, and a nest clip's `source.project` is the id of the nest it shows.

## The graphics summary

`graphics` is a list with one entry for each module in the project's graphics folder, in name order:

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The module's name. |
| `revision` | The module's revision. It changes when the text does. |
| `ok` | `true` when the module compiles. |
| `clips` | The ids of the clips drawn by it, on the timeline and in every nest. |

`ok: false` is the first sign that a graphic clip will draw its error card. See [Graphics with an agent](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/).

The list is empty in a project with no modules, and in a project that has no window.

## Camera Log readback

A file's colour setting is in `color` on its media entry. A file with no setting has no `color`, and each key below appears only when it's set.

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `log` | The curve: `apple_log`, `apple_log2`, `slog3`, `vlog`, `canon_log2` or `canon_log3`. |
| `gamut` | The gamut: `bt2020`, `apple_wide_gamut`, `s_gamut3_cine`, `s_gamut3`, `v_gamut` or `cinema_gamut`. |
| `lut` | The media id of a [LUT](/hdr/log-luts/) used as the conversion, in place of `log`. |
| `detected` | `true` when Frame Job read the setting from the file at import. |
| `pq` | An HDR10 file's peak: `file` is what import read, in cd/m², `from` is where it read it (`max_cll` or `mastering_display`), and `peak` is an override. An empty `pq` still marks the file as HDR10. |

`detected: true` is how to tell a setting the file declared from one a person or an agent chose. Setting the Camera Log with `set_media_color` replaces it and drops `detected`. See [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/).

## The report while a nest is open

While `set_scope` has a nest open, `get_project` reports the nest as if it were the project, so the ids you read are the ones the next edit can name.

- `project.tracks` and `project.clips` are the nest's own.
- `project.canvas` has the nest's fixed size. Its other settings are the project's.
- `project.markers` is empty, because a nest has no markers.
- `project.media` and `project.nests` are still the whole project's, but the open nest's own row under `nests` has no tracks or clips, because they're at the top level here.
- `duration`, `playhead`, `selection` and `in_out_range` are the nest's, measured from its own zero.

Two more keys say where you are:

| Key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `scope_clip` | The nest clip it was entered through. |
| `scope_path` | The trail of nests from the timeline, one `{nest, clip, name}` for each level. |

`scope` is the nest's id, the same number an edit's `scope` argument takes. At the timeline `scope` is `null`, and the two keys above aren't there.

`render_frame` follows the same view and draws the nest at its own size. Opening a nest is a change of view, not an undo step. See [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/).

## Related

- [Tools: projects and history](/mcp/tools-projects/)
- [Units and ids](/mcp/units-and-ids/)
- [Editing inside a nest](/mcp/nests/)
- [A typical session](/mcp/typical-session/)

---
title: "Check the picture: render_frame"
description: "Render one frame of the finished timeline so an agent can see its work, choose the file it writes, draw grade and HDR variants, and measure the scopes."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

`render_frame` draws one frame of the finished timeline, so an agent can see what it has done. It goes through the same composition and compositor an export uses, so the picture is what the file will contain at that moment, not a preview of it.

<AtAGlance
  menu="File ▸ Save Frame…"
  keys="⌥⌘E"
  tools="render_frame"
/>

## Render a frame

With no arguments it draws the frame under the playhead at the canvas's size and writes a PNG to a temporary file.

```json
{ "t": 1200000, "path": "~/Desktop/shot.png", "max_width": 960 }
```

The picture comes back two ways: as an image the model can see, and as a file on disk. The text beside it says what was drawn and ends by naming the file:

```
Frame at 1200000 ticks of a 1920×1080 px canvas, rendered at 960×540 px. Written to /Users/you/Desktop/shot.png.
```

It uses the same writer as [**File ▸ Save Frame…**](/export/save-frame/), so a PNG from either one is identical, byte for byte.

With a [nest](/mcp/nests/) open, it draws that nest at its own size, from its own zero, without the nest clip's position, scale or opacity. It takes no `scope`, so open the nest with `set_scope` to look inside.

| Argument | Type | Required | What it does | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`t`](#t) | integer | No | The moment to render, in ticks. | The playhead |
| [`path`](#path) | string | No | Where to write the file. | A temporary file |
| [`format`](#format) | string | No | `png`, `jpeg` or `heic`. | From the path, else `png` |
| [`max_width`](#max_width) | integer | No | Caps the width in pixels, 16 to 8192. | The canvas's width |
| [`burn_in_timecode`](#burn_in_timecode) | boolean | No | Draws the project timecode over the picture. | `false` |
| [`ungraded`](#ungraded) | boolean | No | Draws every clip as if it weren't graded. | `false` |
| [`selection`](#selection) | integer | No | Draws what an adjustment clip's qualifier selects. | None |
| [`sdr_version`](#sdr_version) | boolean | No | Draws an HDR project's SDR version. | `false` |
| [`waveform`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the waveform. | `false` |
| [`parade`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the RGB parade. | `false` |
| [`histogram`](#waveform-parade-and-histogram) | boolean | No | Also measures the histogram. | `false` |
| [`vectorscope`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | boolean | No | Also measures the vectorscope. | `false` |
| [`vectorscope_zoom`](#vectorscope-and-vectorscope_zoom) | integer | No | 1, 2 or 4. Needs `vectorscope`. | 1 |
| `project` | string | No | The path of the open project to act on. | The frontmost project |

## Choose the moment and the file

### `t`

The moment to render, in ticks, 600,000 to the second. It's rounded to the project's frame grid. Leave it out for the playhead. A time before zero draws the first frame, and a time past the end is refused.

With a nest open, `t` and the playhead are the nest's own time.

### `path`

Where to write the file, for example `~/Desktop/shot.png`. The folder must already exist, because Frame Job won't create one. An empty `path` is refused.

Leave it out for a temporary file. Either way, the last sentence of the text names the file written.

### `format`

The kind of file to write.

| `format` | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| `png` | Lossless, keeping the canvas's transparency. |
| `jpeg` | Quality 0.9. JPEG has no transparency, so a transparent canvas is flattened onto black, and the text always says so. |
| `heic` | Quality 0.9, keeping the canvas's transparency. |

With no `format`, the path's extension decides, and `.jpg` and `.jpeg` both mean JPEG. Any other path writes a PNG.

An explicit `format` wins, and the path's extension is replaced rather than added to, so `{"path": "shot.jpg", "format": "png"}` writes `shot.png`. Only an extension Frame Job knows is replaced: `Talk v1.2` becomes `Talk v1.2.png`, not `Talk v1.png`. A JPEG always ends `.jpg`, so `shot.jpeg` is written as `shot.jpg`.

`jpg` also works as a `format`, and capitals don't matter.

### `max_width`

Caps the image's width in pixels, from 16 to 8192. The picture keeps its shape and is never made larger than the canvas. Leave it out for the canvas's own size.

A smaller frame is quicker to send and to look at. The [scopes](#measure-the-frame) measure the frame as written, so their counts cover fewer pixels too.

## Change what's drawn

These four draw something other than the plain picture. The view switches in the window never reach this tool or an export, so an agent asks here.

### `burn_in_timecode`

Draws the project timecode over the picture, on top of everything, as the export sheet's **Burn in timecode** does. It's the project's own timecode, in the toolbar's spelling. See [Burn in timecode](/export/burn-in-timecode/).

### `ungraded`

Draws every clip as if it weren't graded: Light, Color, wheels and curves neutral, and no look. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Ungraded** gives. See [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/).

### `selection`

Takes an adjustment clip's id and draws what its qualifier selects, in place of grading. It's the picture **View ▸ Show Selection** gives.

- White is fully graded, and black is untouched.
- It's the blurred selection when the qualifier has a blur, and it's multiplied by any matte cutting the clip.
- The clip's strength isn't applied.
- Every layer in front of the clip is left out.
- Where the clip isn't on the frame, the picture is black.

Frame Job won't do this for any other kind of clip. See [Qualifiers](/color/qualifiers/).

### `sdr_version`

Draws an [HDR project's](/hdr/hdr-projects/) SDR version, the picture **View ▸ Show SDR Version** gives. White titles come back near white, and highlights above reference white roll off. It's what the SDR exports and JPEG frames hold.

In an SDR project it changes nothing, and the frame comes out identical. See [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/).

## Measure the frame

Each scope argument measures the frame just rendered through the same analyser as the [**View ▸ Scopes**](/color/scopes/) panel, so the two can't count differently. The text gives the headline figures, and a JSON file beside the image holds the counts, named after it: `shot.png` gets `shot.png.waveform.json`.

The scopes read the frame as it was drawn, so `max_width`, `burn_in_timecode`, `ungraded` and `selection` all change what they count.

If the measurement can't run, the call comes back as an error, but the image is already written and the error names it: "Wrote … but its waveform could not be measured: the GPU pass did not run."

### `waveform`, `parade` and `histogram`

- **`waveform`** measures luma. The text gives the share of pixels clipping high and low.
- **`parade`** measures R′, G′ and B′ the way the waveform measures luma. The text gives the share clipping high and low for each channel.
- **`histogram`** counts R′, G′, B′ and Y′ at 256 levels. The text gives the share clipping high and low, read from Y′.

For example: "Waveform: highlights clipped in 0.4 % of pixels, shadows in 0.0 %; its 256 × 256 counts are in …". A pixel clips high at level 255 and low at level 0.

| JSON key | `waveform` | `parade` | `histogram` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The frame measured | The frame measured | The frame measured |
| `levels` | 256 | 256 | 256 |
| `columns` | 256 | 256 | |
| `counts` | 256 column bins, each 256 levels | The same, under `red`, `green` and `blue` | |
| `red`, `green`, `blue`, `luma` | | | 256 counts each |
| `clipped_high`, `clipped_low` | Pixels clipping | Pixels clipping, by channel | Pixels clipping, by Y′ |
| `marks_high`, `marks_low` | The column bins where at least 0.5 % of the column clips | The same, by channel | |
| `highlights`, `shadows` | Percentages | | Percentages |

### `vectorscope` and `vectorscope_zoom`

`vectorscope` measures Rec. 709 Cb and Cr of the encoded values in 256 × 256 bins centred on neutral, bin 128. The text gives the share of pixels that are neutral.

`vectorscope_zoom` is 1, 2 or 4, like the 1×, 2× and 4× cells on a [vectorscope](/color/vectorscope/) slot, and it needs `vectorscope: true`. Zooming spreads a near-grey picture over more bins. At 2 and 4, a pixel off the plot isn't counted, and the text also gives the share that lie off it.

| JSON key | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `width`, `height` | The frame measured. |
| `bins`, `centre` | 256 and 128. |
| `matrix`, `values` | `Rec. 709` and `encoded`. |
| `counts` | 256 arrays by Cr bin, each indexed by Cb bin. |
| `neutral` | Pixels in the neutral bin. |
| `zoom` | The zoom. |
| `off_plot` | Pixels left off the plot. Always 0 at 1. |
| `targets` | The six 75 % colour targets, `R`, `Mg`, `B`, `Cy`, `G` and `Yl`, each `[cb, cr]` in bins at this zoom, or `null` off the plot. |
| `skin_line_degrees` | The skin line's angle. |

## Read what the answer says

The text always starts with the frame's time and sizes and ends with "Written to …". Anything else worth saying sits between the two.

### Graphic problems in the answer

When a [graphic](/graphics/agents-and-graphics/) in the frame had a problem, the answer names it with its frame and the diagnostic:

- `Graphic "lower-third" failed at frame 12: …`
- `Graphic "lower-third" warned at frame 12: …`
- `Graphic "lower-third" does not compile: …`

A failed graphic draws its error card in the picture.

### Waiting for cutout masks

A clip with [Remove Background](/effects/remove-background/) waits up to 30 s for the masks the frame needs. Frame Job starts making them as soon as the cutout is set, on your Mac.

Past 30 s the clip is drawn whole, and the answer says so: "Clip 12 is drawn uncut: its person masks were not ready within 30 s." For a picture with its subject set to foreground, it says "its foreground masks".

So after setting a cutout, read that sentence before trusting the frame. [`analyze_cutout`](/mcp/tools-framing/) can wait for the masks first.

### A cursor that can't be drawn

A screen recording's cursor is drawn from its cursor file. When the file can't be read, the clip draws without one and the answer says "The cursor of media 5 is not drawn: …".

## Frames from an HDR project

In an [HLG project](/hdr/hdr-projects/), the frame depends on the format:

| What you ask for | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| `png` | 16-bit, labelled BT.2100 HLG |
| `heic` | 10-bit, labelled BT.2100 HLG |
| `jpeg` | The project's SDR version, labelled BT.709 |
| Any format with `sdr_version` | The project's SDR version, labelled BT.709 |

Scopes read the picture drawn. On the HLG picture they read the HLG signal, and on the SDR version they read as an SDR project's do.

On the HLG signal:

- Each scope's JSON adds `signal: "hlg"`.
- The waveform, parade and histogram JSON add `scale`: `unit` (`cd/m²`), `ticks` (each with `percent`, `level` and `nits`), `reference_white_percent` (75) and `clip_percent` (100).
- Luma takes Rec. 2020's weights, and the vectorscope takes Rec. 2020's matrix and targets.
- The text says so. The waveform's reads "reference white at 75 %, 203 cd/m², and 100 % at 1,000 cd/m²".

See [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/) and [Export HDR](/hdr/export-hdr/).

## When it won't render

Nothing is drawn in these cases, and the answer says why.

| It says | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| "No frame at … Either the time is past the end of the timeline, the media is missing, or the timeline is empty." | Check `duration` and `missing_media` in [`get_project`](/mcp/get-project/). |
| "There is no folder at … to write into." | Create the folder, or choose another `path`. |
| "path must name a file to write — omit it for a temporary one." | The `path` was empty. |
| "format must be one of png, jpeg, heic (got …)." | Use one of the three. |
| "max_width must be 16…8192 px (got …)." | Use a width in range. |
| "selection must name an adjustment clip of this project; clip … is not one." | Pass an adjustment clip's id. With a nest open, it has to be in the nest. |
| "vectorscope_zoom must be 1, 2 or 4 (got …)." | Use one of the three. |
| "vectorscope_zoom needs vectorscope: true." | Add `vectorscope: true`. |

## Related

- [Save Frame](/export/save-frame/)
- [Tools: rendering and export](/mcp/tools-render-and-export/)
